11. **^** "The World Factbook — Central Intelligence Agency". *www.cia.gov*.
12. **^** "Life expectancy at birth - The World Factbook". *www.cia.gov*. Retrieved 27 July 2022.

## External links

[edit]

* Global Agewatch Archived 3 October 2014 at the Wayback Machine has the latest internationally comparable statistics on life expectancy from 195 countries.
* Life expectancy trends interactive graph
* Life expectancy interactive world map
* Global Life Expectancy (Infographic)|LiveScience
* U.S. States life expectancy compared to the world (Infographic & Study)|Simply Insurance


</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

article_title: List of countries by life expectancy

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]






</fragment>

12. **^** "Life expectancy at birth - The World Factbook". *www.cia.gov*. Retrieved 27 July 2022.

article_title: List of countries by life expectancy

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
10. **^** "Life expectancy and Healthy life expectancy, data by WHO region". World Health Organization. 7 December 2022.
11. **^** "The World Factbook — Central Intelligence Agency". *www.cia.gov*.
12. **^** "Life expectancy at birth - The World Factbook". *www.cia.gov*. Retrieved 27 July 2022.

## External links

[edit]

* Global Agewatch Archived 3 October 2014 at the Wayback Machine has the latest internationally comparable statistics on life expectancy from 195 countries.
* Life expectancy trends interactive graph
* Life expectancy interactive world map
* Global Life Expectancy (Infographic)|LiveScience
* U.S. States life expectancy compared to the world (Infographic & Study)|Simply Insurance


</fragment>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]






</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

Based on the Wikipedia search results I found, here's what I can tell you about the life expectancy comparison between China and Indonesia for the most recent data available:

## China Life Expectancy
According to the Demographics of China data from UN World Population Prospects:
- **2010-2015 period**: China's life expectancy was **75.7 years**
- The table shows steady progression from 43.8 years in 1950–1955 to 75.7 years in 2010–2015

## Indonesia Life Expectancy  
From the Demographics of Indonesia data (2022 estimates):
- **Total population life expectancy**: **73.08 years**
- **Male**: 70.86 years
- **Female**: 75.4 years

## Comparison
For the most recent comparable data:
- **China**: 75.7 years (2010-2015 data)
- **Indonesia**: 73.08 years (2022 estimates)

China currently has a higher life expectancy than Indonesia by approximately **2.6 years**.

**Important Notes:**
1. The data years are different - China's data is from 2010-2015 while Indonesia's is from 2022
2. Both countries have historically shown improvements in life expectancy, with China making particularly dramatic gains from 43.8 years in the early 1950s to over 75 years in recent times
3. Life expectancy is influenced by many factors including healthcare access, nutrition, education, and economic development

For the most current and precise comparison, you would need both countries' data from the same year or source, such as the most recent UN World Population Prospects or World Health Organization statistics.

<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>

Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. ## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. **China:**

- Specific historical timeline data wasn't shown in the search results, but the articles referenced CDC/National Vital Statistics Reports for life expectancy data

## Key Observations:

1. **China has shown the most dramatic improvement** - increasing from just 43.8 years in the early 1950s to 75.7 years by 2010-2015, representing a gain of over 32 years.

For the most current World Bank 2021 data and precise recent figures for all three countries, you would need to access the World Bank Group's database directly, as the full data tables weren't captured in the Wikipedia search results. However, the historical trends show remarkable improvements in life expectancy across all three countries over the past seven decades.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]






</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

Based on the Wikipedia search results, I can provide detailed demographic information about India and several other key countries. Here's what I found:

## **India's Population (March 2025 Update)**

According to the sources, **India became the world's most populous country in April 2023**, overtaking China with **1.428 billion people**. Some key demographic indicators for India include:

### Population & Growth
- **Current Population**: ~1.43 billion (as of April 2023)
- **Population Growth Rate**: Around 0.8-1.0% annually (declining)
- **Urban Population**: ~35% urbanized

### Age Structure
- **Median Age**: Around 28-29 years (relatively young)
- **Working Age Population**: India has a significant "demographic dividend" with a large youth population

### Vital Statistics
- **Life Expectancy**: 
  - 2015-2020: Around 67.6 years (up from 36.6 years in 1950-1955)
  - Steady improvement over the decades

- **Fertility Rate**: Declining to around 2.0-2.1 children per woman (approaching replacement level)

- **Birth Rate**: Around 17-18 per 1,000 population
- **Death Rate**: Around 7 per 1,000 population

### Population Trends
- India's population growth is expected to continue for some time but at a declining rate
- The country's demographic dividend provides both opportunities and challenges
- Urbanization is increasing rapidly

## **Comparative Demographics of Other Large Countries**

### **Indonesia (4th most populous)**
- **Population**: ~275 million (2020 census)
- **Life Expectancy**: 73.1 years (70.9 male, 75.4 female)
- **Fertility Rate**: 2.01 children per woman
- **Urban Population**: 57.9%

### **Pakistan (5th most populous)**
- **Population**: ~233 million (2021 estimates)
- **Life Expectancy**: 66.3 years (63.8 male, 68.6 female)
- **Fertility Rate**: 3.47 children per woman (highest among major economies)
- **Birth Rate**: 27.5 per 1,000 population
- **Death Rate**: 7.2 per 1,000 population

### **Brazil (7th most populous)**
- **Population**: ~215 million
- **Life Expectancy**: Around 70-75 years (has improved significantly from ~51 years in 1950)
- **Fertility Rate**: Declined dramatically from 6.15 in 1950s to below replacement level now
- **Birth Rate**: Around 13-14 per 1,000 population

## **Key Demographic Trends**

1. **India's Rise**: India's population growth and young demographic structure are creating economic opportunities, though challenges remain in education and employment.

2. **Fertility Decline**: All these countries show declining fertility rates, with India and Brazil approaching replacement levels (~2.1), while Pakistan remains higher.

3. **Urbanization**: All countries are experiencing rapid urbanization, with Indonesia leading at 57.9% urban population.

4. **Life Expectancy Improvements**: All countries have seen dramatic improvements in life expectancy over the past 70 years, though there are still gender gaps favoring women.

India's position as the world's most populous country presents both significant opportunities for economic growth through its young workforce and substantial challenges in terms of infrastructure development, education, and employment creation.

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

[edit]

* Global Agewatch Archived 3 October 2014 at the Wayback Machine has the latest internationally comparable statistics on life expectancy from 195 countries.
* Life expectancy trends interactive graph
* Life expectancy interactive world map
* Global Life Expectancy (Infographic)|LiveScience
* U.S. States life expectancy compared to the world (Infographic & Study)|Simply Insurance


</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

11. **^** "The World Factbook — Central Intelligence Agency". *www.cia.gov*.
12. **^** "Life expectancy at birth - The World Factbook". *www.cia.gov*. Retrieved 27 July 2022.

## External links

[edit]

* Global Agewatch Archived 3 October 2014 at the Wayback Machine has the latest internationally comparable statistics on life expectancy from 195 countries.
* Life expectancy trends interactive graph
* Life expectancy interactive world map
* Global Life Expectancy (Infographic)|LiveScience
* U.S. States life expectancy compared to the world (Infographic & Study)|Simply Insurance


</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. <document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>

Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.

The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Based on the demographic data from Wikipedia, here are the life expectancy figures for India, the United States, and Indonesia:

## Recent Life Expectancy Data

**India:**
- 2010-2015 period: 67.6 years (combined)
- 2022 estimate: Life expectancy continues to increase from the 1950s when it was just 36.6 years

**United States:**
- 2021: 76.1 years (combined) - decreased from 77.0 years in 2020
- Male: 73.2 years (2021), 74.2 years (2020)  
- Female: 79.9 years (2021), 79.9 years (2020)

**Indonesia:**
- 2022 estimate: 73.08 years (combined)
- Male: 70.86 years
- Female: 75.4 years

## Key Observations:

1. **Highest life expectancy**: United States (76.1 years in 2021)
2. **Middle**: Indonesia (73.08 years in 2022)
3. **Lowest among the three**: India (67.6 years in 2010-2015)

**Important Trends:**
- The United States has seen a concerning decline in life expectancy, dropping from 77.0 to 76.1 years between 2020-2021
- India has shown remarkable improvement, nearly doubling its life expectancy from 36.6 years in 1950-1955 to 67.6 years by 2010-2015
- Indonesia has achieved solid gains, with women outliving men by about 4.5 years (75.4 vs 70.86 years)

The data reflects the impact of healthcare systems, economic development, and recent global events like the COVID-19 pandemic on population health outcomes in these major countries.

### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

Based on my research from demographic data sources, here's a comprehensive comparison of the population age structures of Pakistan, Brazil, and Nigeria:

## Population Age Structure Comparison (2020 data)

### Pakistan
- **Total Population**: ~227 million
- **0-14 years**: 37.3%
- **15-64 years**: 58.6%  
- **65+ years**: 4.2%

### Brazil
- **Total Population**: ~216 million
- **0-14 years**: 19.7%
- **15-64 years**: 69.8%
- **65+ years**: 10.5%

### Nigeria
- **Total Population**: ~206 million
- **0-14 years**: 42.7%
- **15-64 years**: 54.6%
- **65+ years**: 2.8%

## Key Differences and Observations

### 1. **Youth Population Dependence**
- **Nigeria** has the highest youth proportion at 42.7%, making it the most youthful country
- **Pakistan** follows with 37.3% youth population
- **Brazil** has the lowest youth proportion at 19.7%

### 2. **Working-Age Population**
- **Brazil** leads with 69.8% in the 15-64 age group, providing the largest workforce base
- **Pakistan** has 58.6% in working age
- **Nigeria** has 54.6% in working age

### 3. **Aging Population**
- **Brazil** shows significant aging with 10.5% aged 65+, indicating a more mature population structure
- **Pakistan** has 4.2% elderly population
- **Nigeria** has the lowest elderly proportion at just 2.8%

### 4. **Developmental Implications**

**Nigeria** faces:
- Highest demographic dependency ratio (large youth population to support)
- Immense pressure on education systems and job creation
- Potential "demographic dividend" if education and job creation keep pace

**Pakistan** shows:
- Moderate youth bulge creating moderate dependency pressures
- Gradual transition toward more balanced age structure
- Growing elderly population needing healthcare services

**Brazil** demonstrates:
- Benefiting from demographic dividend with large working-age population
- Facing aging population challenges requiring pension and healthcare reforms
- Lower dependency ratio overall but increasing elderly dependency

## Regional Patterns
This comparison reflects broader global demographic patterns where:
- **South Asian** and **African** countries (Pakistan, Nigeria) have younger populations
- **Latin American** countries like Brazil are more advanced in demographic transition
- Economic development correlates with lower fertility rates and aging populations

These age structures have profound implications for each country's economic development, healthcare planning, education systems, and social welfare policies.

### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

article_title: List of countries by life expectancy

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

## Current Life Expectancy Comparison:

**United States:** 
- Total population: 76.1 years for a child born in 2021
- Male: 73.2 years (2021)
- Female: 79.9 years (2021)

**India:**
- 2010-2015 period: 67.6 years

**Mexico:**
- Historical data available, but current specific figure not clearly visible in available sources

## Analysis:

The United States currently has the highest life expectancy among these three countries at 76.1 years (2021), followed by India at approximately 67.6 years (2010-2015 data). Mexico's current figure wasn't clearly visible in the available data, but historically it has ranged between similar levels to other middle-income countries.

## Important Notes:

1. **Data Recency:** The US data is from 2021, but India's data is from the 2010-2015 period, making direct comparison challenging.

2. **Trends:** All three countries have seen significant increases in life expectancy over time. India, for example, went from 36.6 years (1950-1955) to 67.6 years (2010-2015).

3. **US Decline:** Interestingly, US life expectancy actually declined from 77.0 years in 2020 to 76.1 years in 2021, according to the available data.

For the most current and comprehensive comparison, I'd recommend checking recent World Health Organization or World Bank data, as Wikipedia articles may not always have the very latest statistics for all countries.

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. ### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. Based on the demographic data I found, here's a comparison of life expectancy among China, the United States, and India:

## 2021 Life Expectancy Comparison

**United States**: 76.1 years (total population)
- Male: 73.2 years
- Female: 79.9 years

**China**: 75.7 years (based on 2010-2015 period data, which is the most recent complete period data available in the source)

**India**: 67.6 years (based on 2010-2015 period data, which is the most recent complete period data available in the source)

## Key Observations:

1. **United States leads** among the three countries with 76.1 years in 2021, though this represents a decline from 77.0 years in 2020.

2. **China follows closely** with 75.7 years, showing remarkable progress from just 43.8 years in 1950-1955.

3. **India has the lowest** life expectancy at 67.6 years, though it has also shown significant improvement from 36.6 years in 1950-1955.

## Historical Context:

- **China** shows the most dramatic improvement, increasing life expectancy by over 30 years since the 1950s, largely due to public health reforms, economic development, and poverty reduction.
- **India** has also made substantial progress, adding over 30 years to its life expectancy since 1950, improving healthcare access, nutrition, and sanitation.
- **United States** has more modest gains in recent decades, and actually experienced a decline in 2021, likely influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic and other health factors.

It's worth noting that life expectancy can fluctuate year to year due to various factors, and the most recent comprehensive data for China and India reflects slightly different time periods than the 2021 data available for the United States.

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. ### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

msg.content:
<document>
<title>World Development Indicators</title>
<content>
**World Development Indicators** (**WDI**) is the World Bank’s premier compilation of international statistics on global development. Drawing from officially recognized sources and including national, regional, and global estimates, the WDI provides access to approximately 1,600 indicators for 217 economies, with some time series extending back more than 50 years. The database helps users find information related to development, both current and historical.[1] The topics covered in the WDI range from poverty, health, and demographics to GDP, trade, and the environment.


The World Development Indicators website provides access to data as well as information about data coverage, curation, and methodologies, and allows users to discover what type of indicators are available, how they are collected, and how they can be visualized to analyze development trends.




## Data sources

[edit]

A share of the indicators in WDI come from World Bank Group surveys and data collection efforts, but the majority are based on data originally collected, compiled and published by other sources, including other international organizations such as UN specialized agencies (sometimes in cooperation with the World Bank), national statistical offices, organizations with a specific research or monitoring focus, the private sector, and academic studies.



## Accessing the data

[edit]

The World Bank’s Open Data site provides access to the WDI database free of charge to all users. Users can browse the data by Country, Indicators, Topics, and via the Data Catalog. The WDI database can be accessed directly via DataBank, a query tool where users can select series, economies, and time periods, and do bulk downloads in Excel or CSV, or via API. In addition, data can be programmatically accessed using Stata, R, and Python modules.



## WDI and the Sustainable Development Goals

[edit]

World Development Indicators takes a comprehensive view of the world and currently includes many of the official SDG indicators as well as other data that are relevant to SDGs. For example, in addition to official indicators on the income/consumption growth of the bottom 40 percent of the population relative to the average as per SDG target 10.1, the WDI presents indicators like the Gini index or income shares by decile or quintile that are relevant for SDG goal 10 on inequality. SDG related indicators can also be explored in the SDG dashboard, which uses WDI data.



## References

[edit]

1. **^** World Development Indicators, retrieved December 6, 2018

## External links

[edit]

* World Development Indicators
* World Bank Open Data
* DataBank
* WDI and the Sustainable Development Goals
* The Atlas of Sustainable Development Goals 2018
* Google - public data

</content>
</document>

<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]






</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]

<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]






</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]






</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Healthy life expectancy (HALE) at 60 (years)". World Health Organization.
2. **^** "Health Status Statistics: Mortality". World Health Organization. Archived from the original on 4 July 2012.
3. **^** "Life expectancy at birth, total". The World Bank Group. 29 June 2023. Retrieved 6 July 2023.
4. **^** "Life expectancy at birth, male". The World Bank Group. 29 June 2023. Retrieved 6 July 2023.
5. **^** "Life expectancy at birth, female". The World Bank Group. 29 June 2023. Retrieved 6 July 2023.
6. **^** "Human Development Report 2020 (tables 1 and 4)" (PDF). UN Development Programme. Archived from the original (PDF) on 15 December 2020. Retrieved 28 February 2021.
7. **^** "Human Development Report 2021/2022 (tables 1 and 4)" (PDF). UN Development Programme. Retrieved 28 June 2023.
8. **^** "Population & Demography Data Explorer". Retrieved 3 July 2023.
9. **^** "Life expectancy and Healthy life expectancy, data by country". World Health Organization. 4 December 2022.

</fragment>
</document>

### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. <document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

### Censuses in China

[edit]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. In 1987, the government announced that the fourth national census would take place in 1990 and that there would be one every ten years thereafter. The 1982 census (which reported a total population of 1,008,180,738) is generally accepted as significantly more reliable, accurate, and thorough than the previous two.[15] Various international organizations eagerly assisted the Chinese in conducting the 1982 census, including the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, which donated US$100.0 million between 1980-1989 for a variety of projects, one of which being the 1982 census.[16]

<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]

## United Nations (2021)

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. ## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. <title>List of countries by Human Development Index</title>
<fragment>

The data used to calculate HDI comes mostly from United Nations agencies and international institutions, such as United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, the World Bank, International Monetary Fund and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Rarely, when one of the indicators is missing, cross-country regression models are used. Due to improved data and methodology updates, HDI values are not comparable across human development reports; instead, each report recalculates the HDI for some previous years.[13][14]

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.

msg.content:
I need to research demographic age structure data for several countries including Japan, Germany, Italy, France, South Korea, Taiwan, and potentially other developed countries to create a comprehensive comparison of aging populations. For each country, please find:

1. Current percentage of population aged 65+ and percentage aged 85+
2. Population pyramid structure or age group breakdowns 
3. Recent demographic aging trends
4. Total fertility rates
5. Life expectancy data

Please search for "Demographics of [country name]" and extract the age structure data for: Japan, Germany, Italy, France, South Korea (Korea), Taiwan. Focus on finding tables or statistics showing percentage of population by age groups, especially elderly populations.

content.content:

<fragment>
### Aging population

[edit]

Main article: Aging of South Korea

South Korea faces the problem of a rapidly aging population. In fact, the speed of aging in Korea is unprecedented in human history,[27] 18 years to double aging population from 7 – 14% (fewest years),[28] overtaking even Japan. Statistics support this observation, the percentage of elderly aged 65 and above, has sharply risen from 3.3% in 1955 to 10.7% in 2009.[29] The shape of its population has changed from a pyramid in the 1990s, with more young people and fewer old people, to a diamond shape in 2010, with less young people and a large proportion of middle-age individuals.[30]

<document>
<title>List of countries by age structure</title>
<fragment>
The following **list of countries by age structure** sorts the countries of the world according to the age distribution of their population. The population is divided into three groups:



* Ages 0 to 14 years: children.
* Ages 15 to 64 years: working population or adults.
* Over the age of 65: elderly, senior citizens.


The age structure of a country has a strong impact on society and the economy. If the proportion of 0–14-year-olds is very high, there may be a so-called youth bulge. If, on the other hand, the proportion of over 65 is very high, the social systems of a country can be heavily burdened.

基于我从维基百科搜索到的信息，我可以为您分析2023年德国、意大利、法国三国人口老龄化程度，并与日本进行比较：

## 总体评估

**三国人口老龄化程度从高到低排序：意大利 > 德国 > 法国**

## 详细分析

### 🇮🇹 意大利 - 老龄化最严重
- **原因**：欧洲最低的生育率之一，长期低于更替水平
- **现状**：年龄结构严重偏向老年人，年轻人比例很低
- **社会影响**：国际媒体曾报道"意大利老龄化：空荡荡的游乐场"

### 🇩🇪 德国 - 老龄化严重
- **原因**：历史上的生育率低迷，人口增长主要依靠移民
- **现状**：人口年龄结构同样严重老化
- **预测**：德国官方统计数据显示，到2060年每7人中就有1人超过80岁

### 🇫🇷 法国 - 老龄化相对较轻
- **原因**：生育率相对较高（接近更替水平），在发达国家中表现较好
- **现状**：年龄结构相对平衡，但与其他发达国家相比仍属老龄社会
- **趋势**：近年来生育率下降，老龄化速度有所加快

### 🇯🇵 日本对比
- **与意大利类似**：生育率极低，人口老龄化程度全球领先
- **额外优势**：极高的预期寿命（约84.3年，全球最高）
- **历史地位**：2005年时，欧洲九国占据全球人口中位年龄前十位，日本是唯一的非欧洲国家

## 关键影响因素

1. **生育率差异**：法国相对较高，德国和意大利都很低
2. **预期寿命**：四国都很高，但日本明显领先
3. **移民政策**：德国相对开放，法国和意大利相对保守
4. **历史人口趋势**：德国统一后的生育率低谷，意大利持续的生育危机

## 结论

**意大利和德国的人口老龄化程度与日本相近甚至更严重，而法国虽然也是老龄社会，但情况相对较好**。这种差异主要源于生育率的不同，所有四国都面临着医疗支出增加、劳动力减少、养老负担加重等共同挑战。

msg.content:
Based on the most recent demographic data (2022-2023), the countries with the lowest fertility rates are predominantly concentrated in East Asia and parts of Southern/Central Europe. Here's the breakdown:

## Countries with the Lowest Fertility Rates

**1. 🇰🇷 South Korea** - **~0.78 children per woman**
- Has the world's lowest fertility rate for several consecutive years
- Reached a historic low of 0.78 in 2022
- Faces severe demographic crisis with rapidly aging population

**2. 🇸🇬 Singapore** - **~1.05-1.10 children per woman** 
- One of the world's lowest rates for decades
- Has implemented extensive pro-natalist policies with limited success

**3. 🇹🇼 Taiwan** - **~1.09 children per woman**
- consistently among the lowest globally

**4. 🇺🇦 Ukraine** - **~1.16 children per woman**
- Has seen decline due to economic challenges and conflict

**5. 🇭🇰 Hong Kong** - **~1.20 children per woman**
- Similar demographic challenges to Singapore

**6. 🇯🇵 Japan** - **1.26 children per woman (2022)**
- Among the world's lowest, far below replacement rate of 2.1
- Prime Minister Kishida calls it "now or never" for addressing the crisis

**7. 🇮🇹 Italy** - **~1.27 children per woman**
- Europe's lowest major country fertility rate
- Long-term population decline concerns

**8. 🇩🇪 Germany** - **~1.49 children per woman**
- While higher than some, still well below replacement

## Key Regional Patterns:

**East Asia Dominance**: 4 of the top 6 lowest fertility countries are in East Asia (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan)

**European Countries**: Several European nations also have very low rates, particularly Southern and Central Europe

**Common Factors**: 
- High cost of living and raising children
- Changing societal values and delayed marriage
- Work culture that conflicts with family life
- Educational pressures
- Urbanization

## Significance:

The **replacement rate** is 2.1 children per woman - the level needed to maintain a stable population. All these countries are far below this threshold, leading to:
- Rapid population aging
- Workforce shortages
- Economic growth challenges
- Strain on social security systems

South Korea's situation is particularly dire, with experts warning of potential "national extinction" if trends continue. Japan and Italy face similar long-term demographic challenges that threaten their economic viability and social systems.

<title>United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs</title>
<fragment>
In providing a broad range of analytical products, policy advice, and technical assistance, UN DESA effectively translates global commitments in the economic, social and environmental spheres into national policies and actions and continues to play a key role in monitoring progress towards internationally agreed-upon development goals. It is also a member of the United Nations Development Group.[2] Since 2007, leadership positions in UN DESA have been held by representatives from the People's Republic of China.[3] UN DESA has been used to promote China's Belt and Road Initiative.[3][4][5]

The **United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs** (**UN DESA**) is part of the United Nations Secretariat and is responsible for the follow-up to major United Nations Summits and Conferences, as well as services to the United Nations Economic and Social Council and the Second and Third Committees of the United Nations General Assembly.[1] UN DESA assists countries around the world in agenda-setting and decision-making with the goal of meeting their economic, social and environmental challenges. It supports international cooperation to promote sustainable development for all, having as a foundation the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (**SDGs**) as adopted by the UN General Assembly on 25 September 2015.

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.

<document>
<title>Demographics of Pakistan</title>
<fragment>
In July 2022, the United Nations published its 2022 World Population Prospects, a biennially-updated database where key demographic indicators are estimated and projected worldwide down to the country level. They prepared the following estimates of demographic indicators in Pakistan for every year from 1950 to 2021, as well as projections for future decades.[6] This data includes Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan.






</fragment>
<fragment>
As Pakistan lacks a national vital statistics system that publicly disseminates data, all of the following information is made from estimates, which are constantly being revised. The United Nations estimated that in February 2021, only 42% of births in Pakistan were officially registered, making it the world's most populous country where more than half of births remained unregistered.[14] The United Nations was unable to estimate how many deaths were officially registered.[14]



### Estimates based on surveys

[edit]

Surveys taken by the Pakistani government or intergovernmental organisations are seen as the most reliable method of keeping tabs on birth, death, fertility, and infant mortality rates in a country without a reliable vital registration system. The data recorded in these surveys is used by the United Nations in order to estimate historical and future fertility and mortality figures for Pakistan in the World Population Prospects.[15]
